title: SAP GUI and SAP Fiori – Navigating the SAP World

sections.title: Why learners see two interfaces
sections.text:
In many projects and training systems you will encounter two main ways of
accessing SAP:.

SAP GUI – the classic, desktop-style interface used for decades, especially in
on-premise and ECC environments, and still heavily used with S/4HANA for
certain transactions.
SAP Fiori – the modern, web-based, role-based user experience surfaced
through the Fiori launchpad, designed to be more intuitive and responsive.
SAP GUI SAP Fiori

You may hear things like:
“Run this in the GUI, that transaction still doesn’t have a Fiori app.”
“Use the Fiori app instead—this is how business users will work going
forward.”
Both are valid in real projects. The strategic direction is Fiori, but SAP GUI remains
important, especially for administrative, technical, or legacy processes. As a
consultant, you must:

Recognize both
interfaces on sight.
Know when each is
likely to be used.
Be able to explain them
clearly to non-technical
stakeholders.

sections.title: SAP GUI Fundamentals
sections.text:
What is SAP GUI?
SAP GUI (Graphical User Interface) is the classic front-end program installed
on a user’s computer (or available via certain web options) that allows access
to SAP systems. It presents screens built in traditional SAP technology and is
driven heavily by transaction codes (T-codes).
For many experienced SAP users, SAP GUI is still the environment they know
best. Even in S/4HANA systems, some configuration and technical activities
are performed through GUI transactions.

Main screen elements in SAP GUI
When you log into SAP via GUI, the standard screen typically includes:

Menu bar Standard toolbar
Application toolbar Command field
SAP Easy Access
menu Status bar

Main screen elements in SAP GUI
When you log into SAP via GUI, the standard screen typically includes:
Menu bar – High-level options such as System, Help, Edit.
Standard toolbar – Buttons like save, back, exit, cancel, and other frequently
used actions.
Application toolbar – Context-specific buttons for the current transaction
(e.g., create, display, change).
Command field – Where you can directly enter transaction codes (for
example, FB60, MM01, VA01).
SAP Easy Access menu – Tree structure showing application areas and
transactions.
Status bar – Shows system messages (success, error, warning) and
information such as system ID and client.
As a learner, it is important to practice:
Entering a transaction code in the command field.
Navigating through the menu tree to find the same transaction.
Observing status bar messages after each action.

Basic navigation actions in SAP GUI
Some core actions repeat across almost every transaction:

Enter / Execute – move forward after
filling fields.
Back – step back one screen, keeping
the current session open.
Exit – leave the current application
and return to the main menu.
Cancel – abort the current task.
Save – commit data to the database
(for example, posting a document).

SAP GUI also includes:
Favorites – a personal list of frequently-used transactions or reports.
Search help / value help (often accessed via the small button next to a field or
F4 key) – shows allowed values or master data selections.
In your bridge module, the goal is not to memorize many transaction codes, but
to become comfortable with the environment so that GUI-based instructions do
not feel intimidating later.

sections.title: SAP Fiori Fundamentals
sections.text:
What is SAP Fiori?
SAP Fiori is the design system and user experience approach that SAP uses to
provide modern, role-based apps across devices (desktop, tablet, mobile). Instead
of relying solely on transaction codes, Fiori presents users with tiles and apps on a
launchpad home screen.
Key concepts:
Role-based – users see apps relevant to their job, not a huge menu of
everything.
Responsive – layouts adapt to screen sizes, supporting multiple devices.
Simple and consistent – consistent patterns for lists, object pages, filters, and
actions.
In S/4HANA, especially in cloud deployments, Fiori is the primary UX for business
users, while GUI is still used for certain administration, configuration, and
technical tasks.

Role-based Responsive Simple and
consistent

Fiori launchpad overview
The Fiori launchpad is the entry point for SAP Fiori apps. When you log in via a
browser, you typically see:

User menu / profile Navigation bar
Home page / spaces Tiles Search bar

Home page/spaces – collections of tiles or cards grouped by role, process, or
function.
Tiles – clickable elements representing apps, KPIs, or dashboards. Some may
show counters or indicators.
Search bar – for searching across business objects, apps, or content.
User menu/profile – for settings like language, theme, and logoff.
Navigation bar – for switching between home, apps in use, or other spaces.
Instead of remembering transaction codes, users:

Click on tiles to open apps.
Use search to find relevant
apps or objects.
Navigate breadcrumbs and
hyperlinks inside apps.

sections.title: Types of Fiori Apps
sections.text:
From a beginner’s perspective, it is useful to distinguish:
Transactional apps
Used to perform business activities such as creating or changing documents.
Examples: Create Sales Order, Post Incoming Payments, and Manage Purchase
Orders.
Think of these as the Fiori equivalents or front-ends to classic transactional
processes.
Analytical apps
Used to monitor KPIs, analyze trends, and drill down into data.
Often visualize metrics such as sales performance, stock levels, or overdue
receivables.
These leverage S/4HANA’s embedded analytics and HANA-powered
performance.
There are other types (such as fact sheets) but at the bridge module level, the main
goal is to understand that Fiori is not only about executing transactions; it is also
about seeing and understanding the business through dashboards and reports.

sections.title: Basic Fiori Navigation Scenarios
sections.text:
To become comfortable with Fiori before deep training, learners should practice a
few simple, guided tasks. These can be done in a training or demo system, if
available.
Scenario 1: Logging in and adjusting user settings
Open the Fiori launchpad URL in a browser.
Enter client (if required), user ID, and password.
After login, locate the user icon or profile menu.
Explore Settings to see:
Theme options (e.g., light, dark).
Language settings (if available).
Default home page or spaces.
Objective: Learners should feel comfortable with the idea that Fiori is a web-based
environment they can personalize.

Scenario 2: Opening a simple display app
On the launchpad, identify a tile for a simple app like “Display G/L Account
Balances,” “Display Customer List,” or “Display Material.”
Click the tile to open the app.
Use search or filters inside the app to find a specific example (e.g., by customer
or account).
Observe how information is presented (lists, object pages, tabs).
Objective: Learners understand how to open and use basic display apps without
changing data.

Scenario 3: Using search and filters
Use the global search bar to search for a term (e.g., a customer name, material
number, or document ID).
Review search results grouped by object type (if available).
Within a list, apply filters (e.g., by date, status, company code) to narrow
results.
Objective: Learners see Fiori as a search-driven environment, not just a static
menu.

sections.title: Working with Data in Screens (GUI and Fiori)
sections.text:
Regardless of whether you use SAP GUI or Fiori, the same data concepts appear in
business documents.
Header vs item
Most transactional documents have:
Header data – information that applies to the entire document. Examples:
Document date, posting date.
Company code, sales organization, purchasing organization.
Customer or vendor.
Item data – line-level information that may differ within the same document.
Examples:
Materials or services.
Quantities and units.
Prices and tax codes.
Cost centers or profit centers at line level.
Understanding header vs item is essential when you review or troubleshoot
documents. For example, in a sales order, the header may hold customer and
overall terms, while items specify each product line with its quantity and price.

Mandatory vs optional fields
In both GUI and Fiori:
Mandatory fields must be filled before you can proceed or save.
Optional fields provide additional detail but are not strictly required.
The system usually indicates mandatory fields visually (for example, with a colored
marker or specific notation). As a consultant, you should learn to:
Recognize which fields are mandatory in a standard process.
Understand which might become mandatory due to configuration.
Explain why certain fields are required from a process perspective, not just
because “the system says so.”

Value help/search help
Many fields are linked to value help, which provides a controlled list of valid entries
such as:
Customer numbers.
Vendor numbers.
Material numbers.
G/L accounts.
Company codes, plants, storage locations.
Using value help correctly:
Reduces data-entry errors.
Ensures that only valid master data values are used.
Helps new users discover available options.
In SAP GUI, value help is often accessed via a small button next to the field or by
pressing F4. In Fiori, it appears as a dropdown, search, or popup selector.

Simulate vs Save vs Cancel
Many critical processes allow you to:
Simulate – see expected results (e.g., posting effect, accounting entries)
without committing changes.
Save/Post – commit the data to the database and create a document with an
ID.
Cancel/Back – exit without saving changes.
Learners should understand:
Simulation is useful when you are unsure about the outcome and want to
verify before posting.
Save/post is a real business action and may impact stock, balances, or other
downstream steps.
Cancel/back should be used when you do not intend to create or change
anything.
This is especially important in training systems when practicing P2P, O2C, and R2R
processes, as it reduces unnecessary test noise and teaches responsible system
usage.

sections.title: SAP GUI vs SAP Fiori: How to explain the difference
sections.text:
As a future consultant, you will often need to explain the two interfaces in simple
terms to business stakeholders.
A clear explanation could be:
“SAP GUI is the classic desktop client, heavily transaction-code driven and used
for many administrative and configuration tasks, especially in older or technical
areas.”
“SAP Fiori is the modern, web-based, role-based user experience, where users
access apps through a launchpad with tiles, use search and filters, and benefit
from a more intuitive layout.”
Both connect to the same underlying S/4HANA system, use the same master data,
and support the same business processes, but the user experience and navigation
style differ.
